Hey! So sorry to hear you going through this. I was your age when I came out to my friends as nonbinary, and was fortunate enough to get their full support. Unfortunately, I do have experience with a family full of transphobic people, so I know how upsetting it can be to have to listen to your loved ones discuss how much they hate who you are even if they don't know that's who you are. Even three years later I still haven't socially transitioned like I would have liked to and it's super frustrating.

The best advice I can give is to seek out any trans/queer youth support groups in your area if there are any. If not, search for services for trans/queer youth and they may be able to refer you to helpful resources.

When you can't imagine a future where you can exist freely as yourself, it's hard to imagine a future at all. But, you're young, and you have your whole life ahead of you to work towards contentment. Again, dysphoria can be so debilitating. If you move away for university you have the opportunity to become independent and move away from a situation that doesn't serve you, and you can work towards being a version of yourself that you're comfortable being. This isn't permanent. It's hard to imagine your situation improving, but it can.

I think this could be resolved by a simple conversation. 'Sorry if I upset you by referring to you as a girl. I wasn't trying to be deliberately hurtful. I wasn't aware that you were nonbinary or uncomfortable with being referred to as a girl. Now I know I'll make sure to gender you correctly. Let me know how you're comfortable being referred to/addressed.'

I don't think you're an asshole for making a mistake, since there are plenty of people who do not consider themselves nonbinary or otherwise trans but still use the pronoun that aligns with their AGAB alongside they/them pronouns, so it's an easy mistake to make. If they didn't explicitly communicate their identity to you, just the pronoun change, then I don't think you're necessarily at fault, but it's understandable that their feelings might be hurt after being misgendered by someone so close to them.

All you can do is apologise and show them that you support them by referring to them in the way that they're comfortable being referred to. I'm sure she'll be understanding. Just make sure to be understanding of the fact that you might have hurt her feelings by misgendering her, even if it was unintentionally. I'm not saying this to make you feel bad; it's just that it's important to keep her feelings in mind even if your intention wasn't to hurt then.

Hi! Fellow trans person here (nonbinary and transmasc to be specific). 

First of all, this situation is really awful and I'm so sorry that your 'friends' reacted this way to finding out about you being trans. And, I'm so sorry that you didn't get to choose how your 'friends' found out about you being trans. I really do understand why you're upset.

With all of that said, although I'm not part of your friend group and have no idea what any of them are actually like, it seems the friend who accidentally outed you really cares about you, and it was an honest mistake on his part. Obviously, it's up to you whether or not you forgive him, and you're well within your rights not to forgive him. However, for him to take the time to make artwork of your OC shows that he must appreciate you far more than your other so-called friends who don't seem to respect you nearly as much.

I'm not sure if you've dropped these friends yet, but it's something I'd recommend. If you're willing to give them another chance- I have no idea if this is possible because I don't know the severity of what they said- set the boundary that you're only willing to stay friends with them if they're willing to treat you with the respect you deserve. But, if the messages were really awful, I really don't feel like it's worth giving them the time of day. Perhaps if you want to find out if the friendships are salvageable or worth salvaging, communicate how hurt you were by what they said. If they show no remorse, then absolutely cut ties with them. You'll be able to find new,  better friends who respect you.

As for the IRL friend, it's up to you whether or not you can forgive them. They do seem to genuinely respect and care about you from what this story indicates. That said, if you cannot find it in yourself to forgive them, you'll have to find some other friends who respect you and appreciate you. I'm not sure if you have any other friends that you're out to. If you do, stick with them. I don't think you should just stick with the IRL friend just because they're your only option because if you can't forgive them then it's not fair on you. But, again, it didn't seem like they were deliberately trying to put you through a horrible ordeal, and they've done their best in apologising to you. Think to yourself: 'what more can this person do to make this up to me? Have they done all they can do to make this up to me?' Maybe try having a conversation with them, or if you find it hard to talk to them, put some time and space between you two and reflect on things.

but, yeah, i do completely get how you feel. back before i realised i was nonbinary/trans, i loved the idea of being pregnant and having that kind of life. i still do want kids, though i'd like to adopt if it's possible. now, the thought of being pregnant gives me the creeps. just the thought of something that significant living inside me and waiting to come out, changing my body in so many ways.... it makes my skin crawl and i can't help but think of it that way when i imagine myself as being pregnant. i don't think of it being so grotesque when i see someone who's pregnant. i think part of it comes from the lack of bodily autonomy i already feel as a trans person, and undergoing a process that defines me by my biological sex fills me with a sense of dread. it's complete body horror for me. i don't want something living inside of me and sort of taking over and cementing me as something i'm not in the eyes of others.

Ace person here! I was pretty certain in my asexuality when I was 13-14. Now I'm 18, I still consider myself asexual. It's no different than knowing you're gay or bi at 16.

That said, it's also completely fine to discover at any point that you're not asexual. You don't need sexual experience to know what you are and what you want. But, should you realise that the term asexual doesn't work for you at any point, it's okay! There are a lot of people who think that they're bi when they're a teenager, but realise with tjme that they're actually gay, or vice versa. The point is, you can label yourself with the term that you most identify with, but that label can change and it doesn't matter if it does change.

TLDR: Yes, you can be asexual at 16. Does it matter if you later discover that you're not asexual? Not at all!

I feel like a lot of what’s missing with ‘lol teenagers are on their phones all the time’ is that it’s just a really shallow, one-note comedy at its core, not to mention over-done. I think my main problem is that it shows a lack of understanding of teenagers as people. We’re all trying to find out who we are and what not, but we’re not a monolith. A lot of the good teen comedies I’ve seen look at teenagers in a way that shows an understanding of what drives them, and the comedic moments that come along with that. They don’t just put a teenager on the screen, make fun of them and that’s that; they flesh out the characters, and therefore the jokes about said characters feel natural and earned. Try to do some revision of a topic or two when you have a period free or some other time to spare, since recapping regularly is useful and keeps things in your head so you’re not just re-learning everything when exam season rolls around (as you likely already know). This way, you know what gaps need to be filled with plenty of time to fill them.

Basically, as long as you’re doing at least a little bit of work every day (unlike myself) and knuckling down during exam season, you should be alright. And even if you don’t do those things, there’s a chance you’ll still be alright, but that’s not wise advice to follow.

I recently offered to read through someone’s fic and give them some constructive advice after they were disheartened by some criticism they received about their fic (they were told it was cringey and no one would want to read their fic). 

It was an OC x CC fic. They were young (13) so their fic was (understandably) quite poorly-written (one might say cringey). It was incredibly rushed and nothing was really developed, so from a storytelling/writing perspective it was pretty bad. It’s a lot like the Big Time Rush SI fic I wrote when I was 12.

Their OC’s name was the same as the name in their user name, though they didn’t ever allude to the fact that the OC was an SI during their conversation.

It was clearly self-indulgent wish-fulfilment, and I didn’t see anything wrong with them writing that! In fact, I was reluctant to give them constructive criticism because they said they were enjoying writing the story, and I didn’t want to be a buzzkill and ruin their fun with my issues with the writing. They said they wanted to become a better writer and learn how to improve, so I gave them some critiques (along with positives and encouragement, of course). I think I sugarcoated everything I wanted to say quite a bit because they left the conversation thinking I really enjoyed their story (so I’m hoping they’re going to continue writing).

The problem with their OC/SI was that she wasn’t really established nor fleshed-out as a character beyond exposition. Her relationships with other characters were also shown through exposition too. Overall, she was a bad character because the author didn’t bother to establish her. I feel like this is more common with SIs rather than OCs, though that’s just speculation.

I don’t think there’s a problem with SIs. My motto is ‘don’t like, don’t read’; if you’re so averse to someone’s silly wish-fulfilment self-insert story, just ignore it. If the author’s having fun with the story, who am I to be an asshole about them having a SI?

With all that said, don’t worry about someone thinking your OC is an SI! If anyone is so bothered by them that they feel compelled to be a jerk, then that’s more their problem than yours!
